 Social Security Payments Are Getting a Boost Due to the Iran War
 The Iran War is contributing to higher Social Security payments in 2027.
 By
 Chris Lewis, CEPF 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Oct. 29, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
Retirees who depend on Social Security senior benefits 
will see a bump in their checks for 2027, and the war with Iran could be a major 
reason behind the increase. 
 The Social Security Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) is meant to ensure benefit amounts keep pace with inflation. Since the war 
has disrupted global oil markets and driven inflation higher, the COLA may also 
increase to reflect the higher cost of living. 
Here's what to know if you or a loved one receive Social Security. 
 Get a protection plan on all your appliances
 Did you know if your air conditioner stops working, your homeowner’s insurance won’t cover it? Same with plumbing, electrical issues, appliances, and more.

 What the war means for the 2027 COLA
The 2026 COLA came in at 2.8%, and the 2027 COLA will be 3.6%. The war's effects on energy prices may have contributed to the higher 2027 COLA.
 Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz drove Brent crude 
oil prices past $120 per barrel in spring 2026. In 2022, former Federal Reserve Chair 
Jerome Powell explained that every $10 increase in the oil price drives up 
inflation by 0.2 percentage points and brings down Gross Domestic Product growth 
by 0.1 percentage point, meaning the war's impact on the economy may be 
long-lasting. 
Those impacts were quickly reflected in energy prices. In April 2026, energy prices rose 
17.9% year over year, and in May, energy costs increased 23.5% year over year. 
In May, gasoline prices were 40.5% higher than a year earlier. Energy accounted for more than 60% of the monthly increase in the overall CPI, which rose 4.2% over the preceding 12 months. 
 Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. 
 How the Social Security COLA is calculated
Higher consumer prices contributed to third-quarter inflation, which determines the 2027 COLA. The COLA is based on the increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which the Bureau of Labor Statistics calculates. 
 Only third-quarter data is used, and it's compared with the third-quarter data from the last year a COLA took effect. If the CPI-W has increased, a COLA percentage is applied, and 
benefits increase for the next year. 
 The COLA calculation is based on data from July, August, and September. In October, it was announced that the 2027 COLA would be 3.6%.
 What a higher COLA actually means
At first glance, a higher COLA might seem like a positive change, since it means 
beneficiaries may receive larger Social Security checks in 2027. But a higher COLA doesn't necessarily mean retirees will feel financially better off.
 A COLA isn't designed to outpace inflation, but to ensure that benefits keep up 
with inflation. A 2027 COLA won't take effect until January, meaning retirees must cope with existing inflation rates until then without an extra 
benefits boost. 
 Since the cost of energy, food, health care, and housing is 
already climbing, retirees have many months to go before their benefits may 
increase. That's a long time to stretch a budget that doesn't account for 
inflation.

 Could the COLA come up short
The COLA may not accurately reflect the expenses that retirees face. Since 
retirees often spend a large portion of their budgets on health care, which often 
outpaces inflation, the COLA may not result in a benefits increase large enough 
to keep up with the climbing costs retirees face. 
The COLA calculation also doesn't reflect any inflation that could occur during 
the fourth quarter. As of October 2026, the war with Iran is ongoing, and Brent crude oil prices were over $115 per barrel. Inflation could continue to climb, and the 2027 COLA wouldn't account for increases from October through December. 
 Bottom line
Oil markets are volatile, and there is no clear sign the war in Iran will end before the end of 2026. The 2027 COLA may not keep pace with the price increases retirees experience after the adjustment takes effect.
For now, focus on near-term strategies to help build your financial 
stability. Work to reduce discretionary spending, build up your savings, and 
explore utility assistance programs to save money in 
retirement , rather than counting on the 2027 COLA to close the gap.
